domain: Public Health Policy / Criminal Justice / Political Economy
topic_summary: Analysis of drug policy as a contested kernel with three structural readings: prohibition (criminalize use to protect third parties), harm reduction (accept use while minimizing health harms), and legalization (regulate markets to protect both users and third parties). Each reading instantiates different victim sets and constraint structures, creating irreducible conflicts over whose protection takes priority.

key_entities: Office of National Drug Control Policy (US federal drug policy authority)
People who use drugs (primary affected population)
Harm reduction service providers (syringe exchanges, naloxone distribution)
key_tensions: Individual sovereignty vs social order (freedom to use vs community protection)
Evidence-based policy vs ideological commitment (empirical outcomes vs moral frameworks)
Health paradigm vs criminal justice paradigm (treatment vs punishment)
Harm redistribution vs harm elimination (who bears costs of each approach)
key_mechanisms: Harm reduction services (needle exchanges, naloxone distribution, supervised consumption)
Market regulation (legal supply chains, quality control, taxation)
Racial disparities in enforcement (2.5x arrest rate for Black adults despite similar use rates)
Overdose mortality pathways (unregulated supply, incarceration-linked mortality)
Disease transmission vectors (HIV/Hepatitis C among people who inject drugs)
key_absences: Treatment capacity infrastructure (availability and accessibility of evidence-based addiction treatment)
Economic beneficiaries of prohibition (prison-industrial complex, law enforcement budgets, illegal market actors)
International drug trafficking dynamics (supply-side enforcement, cartel violence, producer country impacts)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The substance-control kernel: the state's authority to regulate individual drug use and market access, grounded in competing claims about legitimate protection of persons and social order
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Legislative/executive power to define controlled substances and enforcement regimes; medical/public health authority to define harm and treatment; judicial authority to adjudicate violations

readings.commitment: State authority to criminalize drug use/possession to protect third parties from drug-related crime and social disorder
readings.authority_grounding: Criminal law sovereignty; moral/paternalistic duty to prevent self-harm and social harm
readings.expected_structural_delta: Users enter victim set via criminalization; third parties protected via deterrence; high enforcement costs; racial disparities in application; incarceration as primary mechanism

readings.commitment: State authority to accept drug use while minimizing health harms through public health interventions
readings.authority_grounding: Public health paradigm; pragmatic acceptance of use as persistent reality; evidence-based harm minimization
readings.expected_structural_delta: Users remain in partial victim set (health harms) but exit criminal victim set; third parties bear disease transmission and crime risks; services as primary mechanism; decriminalization without full legalization

readings.commitment: State authority to regulate drug markets as legal commerce with quality/access controls
readings.authority_grounding: Individual sovereignty over bodily autonomy; market regulation paradigm; elimination of prohibition harms
readings.expected_structural_delta: Users exit both criminal and unregulated-supply victim sets; third parties protected via market regulation; illegal markets eliminated; regulatory capacity as primary mechanism; potential increase in use volume

axiom_contradictions.basis: Prohibition's axiom that state criminalization of use is legitimate protection cannot coexist with legalization's axiom that individual bodily sovereignty prohibits such criminalization. One framework treats use as legitimate state concern requiring criminal sanction; the other treats it as protected individual choice requiring only market regulation.

Prohibition's axiom that deterrence via criminalization reduces use and protects society cannot coexist with harm reduction's axiom that use is a persistent reality best addressed through health services rather than criminal sanction. One framework treats criminalization as protective mechanism; the other treats it as counterproductive harm.

axes.structural_delta: State criminalizes drug use/possession to deter use and protect third parties from drug-related crime and disorder
axes.primary_observable: Arrest rates for drug possession; incarceration rates for drug offenses; self-reported deterrence effects; drug-related crime rates
axes.selection_reason: First reading of contested kernel; highest enforcement costs and victim set size; generates racial disparity mechanisms

axes.human_readable: Harm Reduction Reading (Health Services as Mitigation)

axes.primary_observable: Overdose mortality rates; HIV/Hepatitis C transmission rates among PWID; naloxone distribution coverage; syringe service program access
axes.selection_reason: Second reading of contested kernel; intermediate position between prohibition and legalization; evidence-based outcomes documented

axes.human_readable: Legalization Reading (Market Regulation as Harm Elimination)

axes.primary_observable: Legal market size and tax revenue; illegal market elimination rate; regulatory compliance costs; use prevalence changes post-legalization
axes.selection_reason: Third reading of contested kernel; most structurally transformative; shifts harm from criminalization to market regulation

omegas.description: All three readings redistribute harm rather than eliminate it. Prohibition shifts harm to criminalized users and creates enforcement disparities. Harm reduction accepts use-related health harms while reducing criminalization harms. Legalization may increase use volume while eliminating criminalization and unregulated supply harms. No reading achieves zero-harm state; each makes different trade-offs about whose protection takes priority.
omegas.source: Structural analysis of victim sets across readings

omegas.description: Harm reduction and legalization show consistent evidence of reduced arrests without increased violent crime, and harm reduction shows reduced disease transmission. Yet prohibition persists despite evidence, suggesting ideological commitment or beneficiary entrenchment overrides empirical outcomes. The gap between evidence and policy choice is itself a structural feature requiring explanation.
omegas.source: Research context on evidence base vs policy persistence

omegas.description: Treatment capacity gap (deferred axis) affects all three readings. Prohibition criminalizes users who cannot access treatment. Harm reduction cannot fully mitigate health harms without treatment access. Legalization cannot prevent problematic use without treatment infrastructure. This cross-reading constraint may be more structurally fundamental than the kernel contest itself.

All three readings focus on demand-side policy within one jurisdiction. Supply-side dynamics (international trafficking, producer country violence, cartel economics) are absent from analysis. Legalization in one jurisdiction may not eliminate illegal markets if neighboring jurisdictions maintain prohibition. This absence may invalidate legalization's claimed benefit of illegal market elimination.

Prohibition and harm reduction hold axiom-contradictory positions (criminalization as protection vs criminalization as harm) yet coexist in many jurisdictions as hybrid policy. This suggests either: (1) the axiom contradiction is not absolute in practice, (2) different readings apply to different substances (marijuana legalization + heroin prohibition), or (3) the hybrid is unstable and will resolve toward one reading. The coexistence pattern requires explanation.
omegas.source: Axiom contradiction declaration + empirical policy hybrids

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel decomposition applied as specified. Three readings selected for generation with distinct victim sets and constraint structures. Deferred axes are structural consequences of primary readings rather than independent axes. Omegas document cross-reading tensions and absences.
